title: Shanghai as a Liminal Space: Diasporic Journeys and the Quest for Identity in Meena Prabhu's Chini Mati (The Chinese Soil)
abstract: This paper examines Meena Prabhu’s portrayal of Shanghai in her travelogue, Chini Mati arguing for the city's depiction as a quintessential liminal space—a dynamic, transitional zone facilitating diverse diasporic journeys and profound reconfigurations of identity. Drawing on frameworks from Diasporic Studies, Refugee Studies, and Spatial Theory, the analysis explores how Shanghai's unique historical circumstances—characterized by "lax regulations" and the absence of strict entry requirements like "a passport or a visa"—transformed it into an unprecedented sanctuary. The paper focuses on Prabhu's vivid descriptions of the city as a "mixing pot of the world," attracting individuals such as "Jews fleeing Nazism," "Russian prostitutes," and "lost souls/wanderers from all over the world," who sought refuge or a fresh start away from their "painful history." By providing a haven for the persecuted and a haven for those escaping societal norms, Shanghai fostered a unique environment where traditional identities were shed and new ones forged. This study illuminates how Prabhu's text captures the complex interplay between urban space, migration, and the fluid nature of selfhood, contributing to a nuanced understanding of liminality within postcolonial urban contexts and the broader discourse on global diasporas.

title: Comparing Water Management Trends, Pressures, and Blue City Index of Shanghai and Ulaanbaatar Using the City Blueprint Approach
abstract: Developing cities face growing water challenges that require proactive and adaptive management. Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia experiences severe seasonal water scarcity, limited wastewater treatment, and aging infrastructure, while Shanghai, China as a rapidly urbanizing megacity, faces flooding, pollution, and complex water governance issues. Extreme weather events, including flash floods and prolonged droughts, together with urbanization and climate change, exacerbate these pressures, threatening public health, economic development, and environmental sustainability. This study applies the City Blueprint Approach (CBA) to evaluate and compare water resources management in Ulaanbaatar and Shanghai. Results indicate that the environmental category of the Trends and Pressures Framework (TPF), Shanghai scored 7.3, whereas Ulaanbaatar scored 3.8. Similarly, within the solid waste treatment category of the City Blueprint Framework (CBF), Shanghai achieved a score of 9.3 compared with Ulaanbaatar’s 1.1, representing the largest disparity observed in the assessment. These differences are closely associated with variations in technological development and the distinct environmental conditions of the two cities. The study concludes that adaptive, integrated, and context-specific water management frameworks can improve urban resilience and sustainability, offering lessons for other developing and rapidly urbanizing cities facing similar water challenges. This research places greater emphasis on the BCI results and conducts the comparative analysis primarily based on these outcomes. Shanghai is classified as a water- efficient city (BCI = 5.7), supported by extensive wastewater treatment, expanding tertiary treatment, and more advanced waste management, while Ulaanbaatar is categorized as a wasteful city (BCI = 2.5), reflecting aging infrastructure, inadequate wastewater treatment, and limited climate adaptation capacity.

title: Replication data and code for: Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai
abstract: Derived data and analysis code supporting the manuscript "Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai" (submitted to Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment). CONTENTS data/ — 500 m grid-level derived layers for central Shanghai (n = 1,494 cells): 29 built-environment indicators; commuting carbon outcomes (all-day occupied, morning peak, evening peak); empty-cruising (deadheading) carbon; trip counts, per-trip carbon and short-trip shares; opportunity-accessibility layers; multi-scale (250 m / 1 km) MAUP aggregates; robustness outputs (alternative centre sets, disjoint commuting definitions); external-validation summaries; the 500 m grid geometry (GeoPackage); and full-precision model hyperparameters. code/ — Tier-A analysis scripts that run entirely from the released data with relative paths: OLS / Moran's I / LISA, spatial Durbin model, GWR/MGWR, XGBoost with spatial-block cross-validation, SHAP, ALE, single-variable counterfactual scan, and NSGA-II bi-objective optimisation (F1 = minimise predicted commuting carbon; F2 = maximise opportunity accessibility). code_restricted/ — Tier-B provenance scripts requiring the restricted raw inputs (GPS trajectories, mobile-signalling OD, raw POI); these cannot be re-executed from this package. Their aggregated outputs are included in data/. output/ — Trained models, hyperparameters, spatial fold assignment and cross-validation metrics, enabling byte-level model reproduction. MANIFEST.csv — Full 32-character MD5 checksums and file sizes for every file. README_ZENODO.md — Data dictionary, units, reproduction instructions, and an explicit statement of what can and cannot be reproduced from this package. IMPORTANT — TWO CARBON BASELINES The released carbon fields are computed with the reference emission factor EF = 2.98 kg CO2/L, on which all models were trained. The manuscript reports absolute carbon with a calibrated factor EF = 2.31 kg CO2/L (see Appendix H of the manuscript); grid_500m_carbon_ef231.csv provides these values directly (= released carbon x 0.775). All scale-invariant quantities — percentages, SHAP values, ALE profiles, correlations, Moran's I, accessibility, exchange rates — are identical under either factor. DATA AVAILABILITY AND RESTRICTIONS The underlying taxi GPS trajectories and the mobile-signalling job-housing OD data are provided by third parties under authorisation and cannot be redistributed. Only de-identified, aggregate grid-level derivatives are released here. Consequently the derivation of carbon from raw trajectories cannot be re-executed from this package; the released grid data can, however, be verified for internal consistency and used to reproduce every statistical and modelling result reported in the manuscript. ACCESS Files are restricted during peer review. Editors and reviewers may request access, or use the access link provided in the cover letter.

title: The Impact of Chinese Leadership Style on Pakistani Employees' Performance: A Case Study of Shanghai Electric Thar Coal Power Project
abstract: With the continued expansion of China’s Belt and Road Initiative, Chinese enterprises are increasingly operating in culturally diverse environments, where cross-cultural management challenges have become a critical concern. Among these, the effectiveness of Chinese leadership styles in foreign cultural contexts remains insufficiently understood. This research proposes to investigate how traditional Chinese leadership styles—authoritative, benevolent, and virtuous—affect employee performance in Pakistan, an important partner country under the BRI framework . It also seeks to investigate how perceived support from the organization and cultural intelligence moderate these correlations. This study will use an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design with a focus on quantitative analysis supported by qualitative insights . In the qualitative phase, semi-structured interviews with managers and employees will provide deeper insights into the contextual dynamics underlying leadership effectiveness. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design is adopted, with a primary focus on quantitative analysis supported by qualitative insights. The findings are expected to contribute to leadership and cross-cultural management literature by extending Chinese leadership theory into an Islamic cultural context and by examining the interaction between leadership styles and key moderating factors. Practically, the study aims to provide insights for multinational Chinese enterprises to enhance leadership effectiveness and improve employee performance in cross-cultural settings. Overall, this research will provide both theoretical and practical contributions to understanding leadership effectiveness in international business environments, particularly within the context of China–Pakistan economic cooperation under the BRI.

title: THE ROLE OF UZBEKISTAN IN THE ECONOMIC DIPLOMACY OF THE SHANGHAI COOPERATION ORGANIZATION AND THE ECONOMIC COOPERATION ORGANIZATION
abstract: This article analyzes the role and significance of Uzbekistan in the economic diplomacy of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization and the Economic Cooperation Organization. The study examines Uzbekistan’s economic cooperation within these international organizations, its activities in attracting investments, its role in developing foreign trade relations, and its contribution to regional integration processes. Particular attention is given to prospects for cooperation in transport and logistics, energy, industry, and innovation. The findings indicate that Uzbekistan’s active participation within these organizations serves as an important factor in accelerating economic development, expanding international economic relations, and strengthening the country’s economic position in the region.

title: THE SHANGHAI COOPERATION ORGANIZATION AND CENTRAL ASIA: THE TRANSFORMATION OF THE REGIONAL ORDER BETWEEN MULTIPOLARITY AND ASYMMETRIC INTEGRATION
abstract: This article provides a comprehensive analysis of the role of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in the transformation of the regional order in Central Asia under the conditions of an emerging multipolar international system. Drawing upon the methodological approaches of critical geopolitics and the theory of new regionalism, the author examines the dual nature of the SCO as a platform that simultaneously ensures regional stability and reproduces power asymmetries between the Central Asian states and their larger neighbors—China and Russia. The article identifies the key vectors of the organization’s development, including the expansion of membership, the institutionalization of economic cooperation through the linkage between the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) and the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), as well as the evolution of the security agenda. Particular attention is paid to the strategies of Central Asian states, which employ multivector foreign policies as a tool for preserving autonomy amid intensifying competition among major powers. The study concludes that a hybrid model of regionalism is emerging in Central Asia, in which formal institutions coexist with informal practices of interest coordination, while the SCO functions as a platform that minimizes the transaction costs of regional interaction without transferring sovereignty to a supranational level.

title: THE IMPORTANCE OF THE REPUBLIC OF UZBEKISTAN'S COOPERATION WITH THE SHANGHAI COOPERATION ORGANIZATION IN THE FIELDS OF SECURITY AND ECONOMY
abstract: This article examines the importance of Uzbekistan’s cooperation with the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in economic and security fields. It discusses Uzbekistan’s membership in the SCO, the growth of trade relations, and the expansion of export and import cooperation with member states. The paper also highlights the role of the SCO in strengthening regional transport, energy, infrastructure, and investment projects. In addition, it analyzes cooperation in combating terrorism, extremism, drug trafficking, and cyber threats. The study concludes that SCO partnership supports Uzbekistan’s economic development, regional integration, strategic security, improvement of the population’s socio-economic well-being, and long-term diplomatic interests in Eurasia today.

title: OPTIMIZATION AND PRACTICAL STRACTEGIES FOR EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE EVALUATION IN SHANGHAI GOLDEN CO.,LTD
abstract: Performance evaluation is a core component of an enterprise’s human resource management system and plays an important role in improving employees’ work efficiency, optimizing organizational management, and promoting the achievement of strategic objectives. With the increasing competition in the vocational education and training industry, educational institutions need not only to improve course quality and service standards but also to stimulate employee potential through scientific human resource management practices. Taking Shanghai Golden Co., Ltd (GOLDEN) as the research object, this study analyzes the problems existing in the current employee performance evaluation system of education and training institutions, including issues related to indicator design, incentive mechanisms, and evaluation dimensions. On this basis, the paper proposes optimization strategies for performance evaluation to establish a more scientific, fair, and motivating performance management system, thereby promoting the sustainable development of education and training institutions.

title: PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT OPTIMIZATION AND INNOVATION IN THE DIGITAL ECONOMY: A CASE STUDY OF SHANGHAI GOLDEN CO., LTD
abstract: Performance evaluation is a key component of human resource management, influencing employee productivity, organizational efficiency, and strategic development. In the digital economy, enterprises must integrate digital technologies into management systems to remain competitive, especially in the education and training industry, where service quality and customer engagement depend heavily on human capital. Shanghai Golden Co., Ltd (GOLDEN), a leading professional training institution in China, has expanded rapidly and adopted digital tools, yet its performance evaluation system still shows limitations, including an overemphasis on short-term enrollment indicators and insufficient attention to innovation and qualitative performance. This study examines the existing performance management practices of GOLDEN and identifies key challenges in the digital economy context. It further proposes optimization strategies that emphasize digital integration, innovation-oriented evaluation, and long-term value creation. The findings provide practical insights for improving performance management systems in education and training institutions and support their sustainable development.

title: Comparing Water Management Trends, Pressures, and Blue City Index of Shanghai and Ulaanbaatar Using the City Blueprint Approach
abstract: Developing cities face growing water challenges that require proactive and adaptive management. Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia experiences severe seasonal water scarcity, limited wastewater treatment, and aging infrastructure, while Shanghai, China as a rapidly urbanizing megacity, faces flooding, pollution, and complex water governance issues. Extreme weather events, including flash floods and prolonged droughts, together with urbanization and climate change, exacerbate these pressures, threatening public health, economic development, and environmental sustainability. This study applies the City Blueprint Approach (CBA) to evaluate and compare water resources management in Ulaanbaatar and Shanghai. Results indicate that the environmental category of the Trends and Pressures Framework (TPF), Shanghai scored 7.3, whereas Ulaanbaatar scored 3.8. Similarly, within the solid waste treatment category of the City Blueprint Framework (CBF), Shanghai achieved a score of 9.3 compared with Ulaanbaatar’s 1.1, representing the largest disparity observed in the assessment. These differences are closely associated with variations in technological development and the distinct environmental conditions of the two cities. The study concludes that adaptive, integrated, and context-specific water management frameworks can improve urban resilience and sustainability, offering lessons for other developing and rapidly urbanizing cities facing similar water challenges. This research places greater emphasis on the BCI results and conducts the comparative analysis primarily based on these outcomes. Shanghai is classified as a water- efficient city (BCI = 5.7), supported by extensive wastewater treatment, expanding tertiary treatment, and more advanced waste management, while Ulaanbaatar is categorized as a wasteful city (BCI = 2.5), reflecting aging infrastructure, inadequate wastewater treatment, and limited climate adaptation capacity.

title: Replication data and code for: Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai
abstract: Derived data and analysis code supporting the manuscript "Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai" (submitted to Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment). CONTENTS data/ — 500 m grid-level derived layers for central Shanghai (n = 1,494 cells): 29 built-environment indicators; commuting carbon outcomes (all-day occupied, morning peak, evening peak); empty-cruising (deadheading) carbon; trip counts, per-trip carbon and short-trip shares; opportunity-accessibility layers; multi-scale (250 m / 1 km) MAUP aggregates; robustness outputs (alternative centre sets, disjoint commuting definitions); external-validation summaries; the 500 m grid geometry (GeoPackage); and full-precision model hyperparameters. code/ — Tier-A analysis scripts that run entirely from the released data with relative paths: OLS / Moran's I / LISA, spatial Durbin model, GWR/MGWR, XGBoost with spatial-block cross-validation, SHAP, ALE, single-variable counterfactual scan, and NSGA-II bi-objective optimisation (F1 = minimise predicted commuting carbon; F2 = maximise opportunity accessibility). code_restricted/ — Tier-B provenance scripts requiring the restricted raw inputs (GPS trajectories, mobile-signalling OD, raw POI); these cannot be re-executed from this package. Their aggregated outputs are included in data/. output/ — Trained models, hyperparameters, spatial fold assignment and cross-validation metrics, enabling byte-level model reproduction. MANIFEST.csv — Full 32-character MD5 checksums and file sizes for every file. README_ZENODO.md — Data dictionary, units, reproduction instructions, and an explicit statement of what can and cannot be reproduced from this package. IMPORTANT — TWO CARBON BASELINES The released carbon fields are computed with the reference emission factor EF = 2.98 kg CO2/L, on which all models were trained. The manuscript reports absolute carbon with a calibrated factor EF = 2.31 kg CO2/L (see Appendix H of the manuscript); grid_500m_carbon_ef231.csv provides these values directly (= released carbon x 0.775). All scale-invariant quantities — percentages, SHAP values, ALE profiles, correlations, Moran's I, accessibility, exchange rates — are identical under either factor. DATA AVAILABILITY AND RESTRICTIONS The underlying taxi GPS trajectories and the mobile-signalling job-housing OD data are provided by third parties under authorisation and cannot be redistributed. Only de-identified, aggregate grid-level derivatives are released here. Consequently the derivation of carbon from raw trajectories cannot be re-executed from this package; the released grid data can, however, be verified for internal consistency and used to reproduce every statistical and modelling result reported in the manuscript. ACCESS Files are restricted during peer review. Editors and reviewers may request access, or use the access link provided in the cover letter.

title: Shanghai as a Liminal Space: Diasporic Journeys and the Quest for Identity in Meena Prabhu's Chini Mati (The Chinese Soil)
abstract: This paper examines Meena Prabhu’s portrayal of Shanghai in her travelogue, Chini Mati arguing for the city's depiction as a quintessential liminal space—a dynamic, transitional zone facilitating diverse diasporic journeys and profound reconfigurations of identity. Drawing on frameworks from Diasporic Studies, Refugee Studies, and Spatial Theory, the analysis explores how Shanghai's unique historical circumstances—characterized by "lax regulations" and the absence of strict entry requirements like "a passport or a visa"—transformed it into an unprecedented sanctuary. The paper focuses on Prabhu's vivid descriptions of the city as a "mixing pot of the world," attracting individuals such as "Jews fleeing Nazism," "Russian prostitutes," and "lost souls/wanderers from all over the world," who sought refuge or a fresh start away from their "painful history." By providing a haven for the persecuted and a haven for those escaping societal norms, Shanghai fostered a unique environment where traditional identities were shed and new ones forged. This study illuminates how Prabhu's text captures the complex interplay between urban space, migration, and the fluid nature of selfhood, contributing to a nuanced understanding of liminality within postcolonial urban contexts and the broader discourse on global diasporas.

title: Shanghai residents attitudes towards raccoon dogs
abstract: Human-wildlife interactions become increasingly common in urban areas across all continents and ecosystem types. Depending on the context, human-wildlife interactions can be categorized as harmonious, neutral, or in conflict and raise cultural, economic, and ecological challenges in maintaining urban biodiversity. Understanding the mechanism behind the tolerance of residents to the presence of wildlife is vital to promoting a harmonious coexistence between humans and wildlife in urban environments. To advance our knowledge of this mechanism, we developed a questionnaire to survey residents in Shanghai, China about their knowledge of and attitude towards raccoon dogs ( Nyctereutes procyonoides ), a species whose population is increasing in urban areas. Using 281 questionnaires, we conducted structural equation modeling to examine how relational values, including familiarity with raccoon dogs, perceived benefits and risks, together with residents' trust in wildlife management authorities, interactively influence the tolerance for this species. We found that the residents' familiarity with raccoon dogs positively influenced their tolerance, both directly and indirectly through increased perceived benefits and reduced perceived risks. Furthermore, trust in wildlife management authorities contributed to higher tolerance through perceived benefits. Our results suggested that education about the relational values of raccoon dogs to the public can reduce the traditional negative connotation for this species and promote the coexistence of people and raccoon dogs in the Shanghai urban environment. Based on our understanding of how raccoon dogs were culturally constructed and the willingness of residents to share landscapes with the species, we advocate that relational values play an important role in future urban biodiversity conservation planning. We also advocate for education programs that familiarize the public with raccoon dogs as well as other species, which can turn urban human-wildlife conflicts into harmonious relationships in Shanghai and other urban areas.

title: SANITARY REFORMS IN EAST ASIA IN THE SECOND HALF OF THE 19TH AND THE FIRST HALF OF THE 20TH CENTURIES (HONG KONG' AND SHANGHAI' CASES)
abstract: The aim of the study is to analyze the history of sanitary reforms in East Asia on the territory of two European enclaves (Hong Kong and Shanghai), which became important centers of transit of Western public health theories and practices to China in the second half of XIX - first half of XX centuries. The relevance of the research is conditioned by the necessity of understanding the historical experience of social processes management in complex epidemiological situations and development of Russian society response to new big challenges, connected with epidemic spreading. The novelty of the study consists in clarifying the existing scientific picture of the formation of modern public health management institutions in East Asia during the period from the beginning of European expansion into China to the Japanese invasion. The study was conducted in 2022 using primary sources from digital libraries in London (Wellcome Collection), Hong Kong (Digital Repository of Hong Kong University), and Shanghai (Virtual Shanghai), as well as works by Western and Chinese historians on public health and sanitation in Asia. During the study methods of historical knowledge were used: problem-chronological, comparative-historical, historical-typological. Methodology of social history of public health became the theoretical base of research. The conclusions of the study are as follows. Sanitary reforms began in those parts of East Asia where European influence was strong. At the forefront of the reforms were the British colony of Hong Kong and the international settlements in Shanghai, where Europeans had to adapt to the difficult conditions of climate, the burden of infectious diseases, and constant overcrowding. Rationalizing the management of urban space, they did not try to offer their way of life to the Chinese population, seeing them as culturally backward and unable to assimilate such civilizational achievements as sewage and running water, but under the pressure of economic and epidemiological needs this step was taken. As a result, by the end of the 1930s, Hong Kong and Shanghai had become prosperous cities with relatively good sanitary and epidemiological conditions.

title: UZBEKISTAN - SHANGHAI COOPERATION ORGANIZATION: MUTUAL COOPERATION FOR PEACE
abstract: The Shanghai Cooperation Organization is a unique political structure that has become an integral part of the world from a global, political and economic point of view for more than 20 years. Of course, the location of this organization indicates a lot. It should be noted that the territory of the member states of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization is more than 34 million km², which is 60% of the territory of Eurasia. Its population exceeds 3.4 billion, which means almost half of humanity. The gross domestic product of the member states of the organization is 22% of the world economy. This article describes in detail the work carried out during Uzbekistan's presidency of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and the achievements made at the end of the SCO Samarkand Summit.

title: District-level data and post-processing code for residential-care accessibility and accessibility-demand alignment in Shanghai
abstract: This record provides processed district-level data and post-processing code for residential-care accessibility and accessibility-demand alignment across the 16 districts of Shanghai, China. It includes population counts aged 60 years and older, accessibility estimates for k = 0 and k = 3, normalized indicators, descriptive coordination scores, ranks, relative accessibility-demand types and the focused sensitivity summary. Population inputs originate from WorldPop China 2025 age- and sex-structured population counts, R2025A v1, DOI 10.5258/SOTON/WP00842. The facility inventory covers 693 facilities and approximately 170,000 approved beds with an end-of-2024 temporal reference. Amap driving queries were made on Monday, 11 May 2026, between 00:00 and 06:00 China Standard Time (UTC+08:00), during an off-peak, non-congested period. The code reproduces district summaries and Figures 3-5 from completed district accessibility estimates. It does not rerun the original grid-level accessibility model. The original population rasters, travel-time matrix and original grid-model program are not included in this district post-processing package.

title: Comparing Water Management Trends, Pressures, and Blue City Index of Shanghai and Ulaanbaatar Using the City Blueprint Approach
abstract: Developing cities face growing water challenges that require proactive and adaptive management. Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia experiences severe seasonal water scarcity, limited wastewater treatment, and aging infrastructure, while Shanghai, China as a rapidly urbanizing megacity, faces flooding, pollution, and complex water governance issues. Extreme weather events, including flash floods and prolonged droughts, together with urbanization and climate change, exacerbate these pressures, threatening public health, economic development, and environmental sustainability. This study applies the City Blueprint Approach (CBA) to evaluate and compare water resources management in Ulaanbaatar and Shanghai. Results indicate that the environmental category of the Trends and Pressures Framework (TPF), Shanghai scored 7.3, whereas Ulaanbaatar scored 3.8. Similarly, within the solid waste treatment category of the City Blueprint Framework (CBF), Shanghai achieved a score of 9.3 compared with Ulaanbaatar’s 1.1, representing the largest disparity observed in the assessment. These differences are closely associated with variations in technological development and the distinct environmental conditions of the two cities. The study concludes that adaptive, integrated, and context-specific water management frameworks can improve urban resilience and sustainability, offering lessons for other developing and rapidly urbanizing cities facing similar water challenges. This research places greater emphasis on the BCI results and conducts the comparative analysis primarily based on these outcomes. Shanghai is classified as a water- efficient city (BCI = 5.7), supported by extensive wastewater treatment, expanding tertiary treatment, and more advanced waste management, while Ulaanbaatar is categorized as a wasteful city (BCI = 2.5), reflecting aging infrastructure, inadequate wastewater treatment, and limited climate adaptation capacity.

title: Factors Influencing Consumers' Intention to Avoid Fast Fashion: A Comparative Study of Milan and Shanghai
abstract: The fast fashion industry contributes significantly to environmental degradation, contributing to primary microplastics entering water bodies through synthetic fiber shedding. Understanding consumer intentions to avoid fast fashion requires examining both psychological and cultural determinants. This study explores the factors of consumers’ behavioral intentions to avoid plastic-based fast fashion garments in Milan, Italy (n=151) and Shanghai, China (n=148). Employing an extended Theory of Reasoned Action (TRA) framework that includes environmental concern and biospheric values as antecedents, we investigated how attitude, subjective norms, environmental concern, and biospheric values influence avoidance intentions. Structural equation modeling revealed that all hypothesized relationships were significant in both cultural contexts, with the model explaining 57.9% of the variance in Milan and 76.8% in Shanghai. Notably, the effect of attitude on behavioral intention was stronger in Shanghai (β=0.598) compared to Milan (β=0.494), while biospheric values more strongly predicted environmental concern in Milan (β=0.433) in contrast to Shanghai (β=0.291). The key innovation of this study lies in its comparison of attitudes toward microplastic effects from fast fashion across cultures, revealing that while universal psychological mechanisms drive sustainable consumption intentions, cultural contexts shape the relative strength of value-based versus attitude-based pathways. These findings suggest that interventions to reduce fast fashion consumption should be culturally tailored, focusing on personal attitudes in collectivistic contexts and value-based environmental education in individualistic settings.

title: Built environment and taxi commuting carbon in Shanghai: volume, not intensity, and a definitional-coupling trap
abstract: This repository provides the grid-aggregated (500 m) derived data and analysis code for the associated study on taxi commuting carbon and the built environment in central Shanghai. The package includes data for 1,494 grid cells, reproducible scripts for spatial econometric modelling, machine-learning attribution, counterfactual analysis, and multi-objective optimisation, as well as trained models and supporting outputs. Raw taxi GPS trajectories, mobile-signalling origin–destination data, and raw POI records are not included because they are access-controlled and cannot be redistributed. All released data are aggregated to grid level and contain no individual-level records. See README_ZENODO.md for data definitions, reproducibility scope, software requirements, and file checksums.

title: Built environment and taxi commuting carbon in Shanghai: volume, not intensity, and a definitional-coupling trap
abstract: Replication data and code for the study "Volume, not intensity: a geocomputational framework for attributing taxi commuting carbon to the built environment in Shanghai." This repository contains the grid-level analysis dataset (1,494 cells) and the complete code to reproduce the grid-level results: spatial econometric models (OLS, spatial lag/error, spatial Durbin, GWR), interpretable machine-learning attribution (XGBoost with SHAP and ALE), and counterfactual multi-objective optimisation (NSGA-II) with the decision-variable-independence check. Note: Raw taxi GPS trajectories and mobile-signalling job-housing data are access-controlled and cannot be redistributed. Trajectory-derived quantities (per-trip carbon accounting, commuting identification, deadheading, short-trip shares) therefore cannot be recomputed from this repository; the grid-level analysis on the shared aggregated data and code is fully reproducible.

title: Replication data and code for: Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai
abstract: Derived data and analysis code supporting the manuscript "Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai" (submitted to Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment). CONTENTS data/ — 500 m grid-level derived layers for central Shanghai (n = 1,494 cells): 29 built-environment indicators; commuting carbon outcomes (all-day occupied, morning peak, evening peak); empty-cruising (deadheading) carbon; trip counts, per-trip carbon and short-trip shares; opportunity-accessibility layers; multi-scale (250 m / 1 km) MAUP aggregates; robustness outputs (alternative centre sets, disjoint commuting definitions); external-validation summaries; the 500 m grid geometry (GeoPackage); and full-precision model hyperparameters. code/ — Tier-A analysis scripts that run entirely from the released data with relative paths: OLS / Moran's I / LISA, spatial Durbin model, GWR/MGWR, XGBoost with spatial-block cross-validation, SHAP, ALE, single-variable counterfactual scan, and NSGA-II bi-objective optimisation (F1 = minimise predicted commuting carbon; F2 = maximise opportunity accessibility). code_restricted/ — Tier-B provenance scripts requiring the restricted raw inputs (GPS trajectories, mobile-signalling OD, raw POI); these cannot be re-executed from this package. Their aggregated outputs are included in data/. output/ — Trained models, hyperparameters, spatial fold assignment and cross-validation metrics, enabling byte-level model reproduction. MANIFEST.csv — Full 32-character MD5 checksums and file sizes for every file. README_ZENODO.md — Data dictionary, units, reproduction instructions, and an explicit statement of what can and cannot be reproduced from this package. IMPORTANT — TWO CARBON BASELINES The released carbon fields are computed with the reference emission factor EF = 2.98 kg CO2/L, on which all models were trained. The manuscript reports absolute carbon with a calibrated factor EF = 2.31 kg CO2/L (see Appendix H of the manuscript); grid_500m_carbon_ef231.csv provides these values directly (= released carbon x 0.775). All scale-invariant quantities — percentages, SHAP values, ALE profiles, correlations, Moran's I, accessibility, exchange rates — are identical under either factor. DATA AVAILABILITY AND RESTRICTIONS The underlying taxi GPS trajectories and the mobile-signalling job-housing OD data are provided by third parties under authorisation and cannot be redistributed. Only de-identified, aggregate grid-level derivatives are released here. Consequently the derivation of carbon from raw trajectories cannot be re-executed from this package; the released grid data can, however, be verified for internal consistency and used to reproduce every statistical and modelling result reported in the manuscript. ACCESS Files are restricted during peer review. Editors and reviewers may request access, or use the access link provided in the cover letter.

title: Shanghai as a Liminal Space: Diasporic Journeys and the Quest for Identity in Meena Prabhu's Chini Mati (The Chinese Soil)
abstract: This paper examines Meena Prabhu’s portrayal of Shanghai in her travelogue, Chini Mati arguing for the city's depiction as a quintessential liminal space—a dynamic, transitional zone facilitating diverse diasporic journeys and profound reconfigurations of identity. Drawing on frameworks from Diasporic Studies, Refugee Studies, and Spatial Theory, the analysis explores how Shanghai's unique historical circumstances—characterized by "lax regulations" and the absence of strict entry requirements like "a passport or a visa"—transformed it into an unprecedented sanctuary. The paper focuses on Prabhu's vivid descriptions of the city as a "mixing pot of the world," attracting individuals such as "Jews fleeing Nazism," "Russian prostitutes," and "lost souls/wanderers from all over the world," who sought refuge or a fresh start away from their "painful history." By providing a haven for the persecuted and a haven for those escaping societal norms, Shanghai fostered a unique environment where traditional identities were shed and new ones forged. This study illuminates how Prabhu's text captures the complex interplay between urban space, migration, and the fluid nature of selfhood, contributing to a nuanced understanding of liminality within postcolonial urban contexts and the broader discourse on global diasporas.

title: Ecosystem Services Concept and Terminology as reflected in Shanghai Urban District Master Planning
abstract: In the international scientific literature, ecosystem services (ES) and green infrastructure (GI) have rapidly emerged as promising frameworks for sustainable and resilient urban planning and development. At the science‒policy interface, a knowledge and implementation gap concerning ES and GI exists in many countries. In this paper, we analyse how the ES concept and GI principles are reflected in the narratives, which the Shanghai Master Plan tests to the Master Plans of all nine suburban Shanghai district Master Plans. Based on linguistic preprocessing, we systematically searched for the explicit and implicit references of ES and GI in the official documents. We found 802 relevant text passages and interpreted them according to their context-specific appearance. The analysis revealed that ES are not comprehensively integrated within the Shanghai Master Plan and the district Master Plans of Baoshan, Chongming, Fengxian, Jiading, Jinshan, Minhang, Pudong, Qingpu and Songjiang. The term ES was not explicitly used in any of the Master Plans. Instead, several terms were found that indicate conceptual similarity. By implicitly taking ES into account and prioritizing them, the districts' master plans reflect the characteristics of the natural landscape and land use patterns in their respective administrative areas. While ecological protection has been promoted and GI and ES are implicitly considered in Shanghai's master plans, a complete discursive shift towards a new ecological approach to urban planning, which is consistently based on GI and ES, has not yet been fully achieved in the master plans for all of Shanghai and the suburban districts.

title: EVOLUTION OF THE SHANGHAI COOPERATION ORGANISATION: FROM THE "SHANGHAI FIVE" TO A MULTIFUNCTIONAL INTERNATIONAL ORGANISATION
abstract: The evolution of the SCO from a border confidence-building mechanism to a multifunctional intergovernmental organisation is examined. The stages of the “Shanghai Five”, the establishment of the SCO, institutionalisation, the expansion of functions and membership, and the strategic renewal of 2025-2026 are identified. It is shown that the organisation developed through consensus, permanent bodies and sectoral coordination without transferring sovereign powers to supranational structures.

title: PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT OPTIMIZATION AND INNOVATION IN THE DIGITAL ECONOMY: A CASE STUDY OF SHANGHAI GOLDEN CO., LTD
abstract: Performance evaluation is a key component of human resource management, influencing employee productivity, organizational efficiency, and strategic development. In the digital economy, enterprises must integrate digital technologies into management systems to remain competitive, especially in the education and training industry, where service quality and customer engagement depend heavily on human capital. Shanghai Golden Co., Ltd (GOLDEN), a leading professional training institution in China, has expanded rapidly and adopted digital tools, yet its performance evaluation system still shows limitations, including an overemphasis on short-term enrollment indicators and insufficient attention to innovation and qualitative performance. This study examines the existing performance management practices of GOLDEN and identifies key challenges in the digital economy context. It further proposes optimization strategies that emphasize digital integration, innovation-oriented evaluation, and long-term value creation. The findings provide practical insights for improving performance management systems in education and training institutions and support their sustainable development.

title: LEADERSHIP SUCCESSION AND STRATEGIC CONTINUITY: A CASE STUDY OF SHANGHAI MODEL ORGANISMS CENTER, INC
abstract: Strategic continuity is a critical concern for pharmaceutical enterprises operating in knowledge-intensive and highly regulated environments. Leadership succession, if poorly managed, may interrupt long-term research agendas, weaken governance stability, and undermine organizational performance. This study examines the relationship between leadership succession and strategic continuity through a case study of Shanghai Model Organisms Center, Inc. Drawing on succession planning theory and strategic management literature, this research adopts a qualitative case study approach based on secondary data analysis. The findings indicate that structured leadership succession mechanisms contribute to strategic continuity by preserving organizational vision, stabilizing decision-making processes, and safeguarding key knowledge assets. The study offers practical implications for pharmaceutical enterprises seeking to manage leadership transitions without compromising long-term strategic objectives.

title: Visual Information and Geographic Reliability in Residential Valuation: A Multimodal, Multi-Source Benchmark from Shanghai — analysis code and aggregate results
abstract: Companion analysis code and aggregate results for “Visual Information and Geographic Reliability in Residential Valuation: A Multimodal, Multi-Source Benchmark from Shanghai” by Cong Xu, Xinwei Gao and Jinglan Hu. Version 1.0.0. This deposit contains 22 analysis scripts, aggregate model/fold/protocol metrics, calibration and spatial residual diagnostics, measurement and external linkage summaries, extended predictor and temporal evaluation results, data dictionaries, provenance, and a Python standard-library replay script. The primary benchmark evaluates 17,716 Shanghai residential community records across 16 districts and 14,908 image footprints. The public replay checks aggregate consistency and package integrity; it does not retrain models or reconstruct individual predictions. Raw community and transaction records, exact locations, third-party RGB/GIS inputs, image patches and embeddings, row-level predictions and split assignments, and model weights are excluded because redistribution rights were not established. A distance-risk bin with n=1 is suppressed. See DATA_ACCESS.md for the source and access boundaries. This is a code and aggregate-results deposit, not a fully open raw-data replication package. Mixed-date predictors and unresolved source dates limit prospective and causal interpretations. Licensing: author-generated aggregate data and documentation are CC BY 4.0; analysis/replay code is MIT. These licences do not extend to excluded third-party inputs or dependencies. AI-assisted development with ChatGPT/Codex and Claude is documented in the package. Funding: National Social Science Fund of China, General Project, grant 24BJY144. Research contact: xuc14@qdhhc.edu.cn.

title: Processed grid-level data for bird-related sentiment and environmental variables in Shanghai, 2022–2024
abstract: This dataset contains processed and anonymized grid-level data used to support the manuscript entitled "Spatial patterns of the bird-related sentiment index and its nonlinear environmental associations: Evidence from social media and explainable machine learning". The shared materials include the 500 m × 500 m grid-level bird-related sentiment index, comment counts, grid-level environmental variables, metadata, data dictionaries, grid-level reference information, anonymized comment-level sentiment scores, and links to publicly available environmental and spatial datasets. Raw Weibo data are not included because they are subject to Weibo platform terms of service and may contain potentially identifiable user-generated information. The original post text, user identifiers, Weibo IDs, exact geotagged coordinates, precise timestamps, user profile information, and post URLs have been excluded from this repository.

title: Built environment and taxi commuting carbon in Shanghai: volume, not intensity, and a definitional-coupling trap
abstract: This repository provides the grid-aggregated (500 m) derived data and analysis code for the associated study on taxi commuting carbon and the built environment in central Shanghai. The package includes data for 1,494 grid cells, reproducible scripts for spatial econometric modelling, machine-learning attribution, counterfactual analysis, and multi-objective optimisation, as well as trained models and supporting outputs. Raw taxi GPS trajectories, mobile-signalling origin–destination data, and raw POI records are not included because they are access-controlled and cannot be redistributed. All released data are aggregated to grid level and contain no individual-level records. See README_ZENODO.md for data definitions, reproducibility scope, software requirements, and file checksums.

title: Built environment and taxi commuting carbon in Shanghai: volume, not intensity, and a definitional-coupling trap
abstract: Replication data and code for the study "Volume, not intensity: a geocomputational framework for attributing taxi commuting carbon to the built environment in Shanghai." This repository contains the grid-level analysis dataset (1,494 cells) and the complete code to reproduce the grid-level results: spatial econometric models (OLS, spatial lag/error, spatial Durbin, GWR), interpretable machine-learning attribution (XGBoost with SHAP and ALE), and counterfactual multi-objective optimisation (NSGA-II) with the decision-variable-independence check. Note: Raw taxi GPS trajectories and mobile-signalling job-housing data are access-controlled and cannot be redistributed. Trajectory-derived quantities (per-trip carbon accounting, commuting identification, deadheading, short-trip shares) therefore cannot be recomputed from this repository; the grid-level analysis on the shared aggregated data and code is fully reproducible.

title: Replication data and code for: Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai
abstract: Derived data and analysis code supporting the manuscript "Volume, not intensity: built environment and taxi peak-commuting carbon in central Shanghai" (submitted to Transportation Research Part D: Transport and Environment). CONTENTS data/ — 500 m grid-level derived layers for central Shanghai (n = 1,494 cells): 29 built-environment indicators; commuting carbon outcomes (all-day occupied, morning peak, evening peak); empty-cruising (deadheading) carbon; trip counts, per-trip carbon and short-trip shares; opportunity-accessibility layers; multi-scale (250 m / 1 km) MAUP aggregates; robustness outputs (alternative centre sets, disjoint commuting definitions); external-validation summaries; the 500 m grid geometry (GeoPackage); and full-precision model hyperparameters. code/ — Tier-A analysis scripts that run entirely from the released data with relative paths: OLS / Moran's I / LISA, spatial Durbin model, GWR/MGWR, XGBoost with spatial-block cross-validation, SHAP, ALE, single-variable counterfactual scan, and NSGA-II bi-objective optimisation (F1 = minimise predicted commuting carbon; F2 = maximise opportunity accessibility). code_restricted/ — Tier-B provenance scripts requiring the restricted raw inputs (GPS trajectories, mobile-signalling OD, raw POI); these cannot be re-executed from this package. Their aggregated outputs are included in data/. output/ — Trained models, hyperparameters, spatial fold assignment and cross-validation metrics, enabling byte-level model reproduction. MANIFEST.csv — Full 32-character MD5 checksums and file sizes for every file. README_ZENODO.md — Data dictionary, units, reproduction instructions, and an explicit statement of what can and cannot be reproduced from this package. IMPORTANT — TWO CARBON BASELINES The released carbon fields are computed with the reference emission factor EF = 2.98 kg CO2/L, on which all models were trained. The manuscript reports absolute carbon with a calibrated factor EF = 2.31 kg CO2/L (see Appendix H of the manuscript); grid_500m_carbon_ef231.csv provides these values directly (= released carbon x 0.775). All scale-invariant quantities — percentages, SHAP values, ALE profiles, correlations, Moran's I, accessibility, exchange rates — are identical under either factor. DATA AVAILABILITY AND RESTRICTIONS The underlying taxi GPS trajectories and the mobile-signalling job-housing OD data are provided by third parties under authorisation and cannot be redistributed. Only de-identified, aggregate grid-level derivatives are released here. Consequently the derivation of carbon from raw trajectories cannot be re-executed from this package; the released grid data can, however, be verified for internal consistency and used to reproduce every statistical and modelling result reported in the manuscript. ACCESS Files are restricted during peer review. Editors and reviewers may request access, or use the access link provided in the cover letter.

title: LEADERSHIP SUCCESSION AND STRATEGIC CONTINUITY: A CASE STUDY OF SHANGHAI MODEL ORGANISMS CENTER, INC
abstract: Strategic continuity is a critical concern for pharmaceutical enterprises operating in knowledge-intensive and highly regulated environments. Leadership succession, if poorly managed, may interrupt long-term research agendas, weaken governance stability, and undermine organizational performance. This study examines the relationship between leadership succession and strategic continuity through a case study of Shanghai Model Organisms Center, Inc. Drawing on succession planning theory and strategic management literature, this research adopts a qualitative case study approach based on secondary data analysis. The findings indicate that structured leadership succession mechanisms contribute to strategic continuity by preserving organizational vision, stabilizing decision-making processes, and safeguarding key knowledge assets. The study offers practical implications for pharmaceutical enterprises seeking to manage leadership transitions without compromising long-term strategic objectives.

title: Shanghai as a Liminal Space: Diasporic Journeys and the Quest for Identity in Meena Prabhu's Chini Mati (The Chinese Soil)
abstract: This paper examines Meena Prabhu’s portrayal of Shanghai in her travelogue, Chini Mati arguing for the city's depiction as a quintessential liminal space—a dynamic, transitional zone facilitating diverse diasporic journeys and profound reconfigurations of identity. Drawing on frameworks from Diasporic Studies, Refugee Studies, and Spatial Theory, the analysis explores how Shanghai's unique historical circumstances—characterized by "lax regulations" and the absence of strict entry requirements like "a passport or a visa"—transformed it into an unprecedented sanctuary. The paper focuses on Prabhu's vivid descriptions of the city as a "mixing pot of the world," attracting individuals such as "Jews fleeing Nazism," "Russian prostitutes," and "lost souls/wanderers from all over the world," who sought refuge or a fresh start away from their "painful history." By providing a haven for the persecuted and a haven for those escaping societal norms, Shanghai fostered a unique environment where traditional identities were shed and new ones forged. This study illuminates how Prabhu's text captures the complex interplay between urban space, migration, and the fluid nature of selfhood, contributing to a nuanced understanding of liminality within postcolonial urban contexts and the broader discourse on global diasporas.

title: The Impact of Chinese Leadership Style on Pakistani Employees' Performance: A Case Study of Shanghai Electric Thar Coal Power Project
abstract: With the continued expansion of China’s Belt and Road Initiative, Chinese enterprises are increasingly operating in culturally diverse environments, where cross-cultural management challenges have become a critical concern. Among these, the effectiveness of Chinese leadership styles in foreign cultural contexts remains insufficiently understood. This research proposes to investigate how traditional Chinese leadership styles—authoritative, benevolent, and virtuous—affect employee performance in Pakistan, an important partner country under the BRI framework . It also seeks to investigate how perceived support from the organization and cultural intelligence moderate these correlations. This study will use an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design with a focus on quantitative analysis supported by qualitative insights . In the qualitative phase, semi-structured interviews with managers and employees will provide deeper insights into the contextual dynamics underlying leadership effectiveness. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design is adopted, with a primary focus on quantitative analysis supported by qualitative insights. The findings are expected to contribute to leadership and cross-cultural management literature by extending Chinese leadership theory into an Islamic cultural context and by examining the interaction between leadership styles and key moderating factors. Practically, the study aims to provide insights for multinational Chinese enterprises to enhance leadership effectiveness and improve employee performance in cross-cultural settings. Overall, this research will provide both theoretical and practical contributions to understanding leadership effectiveness in international business environments, particularly within the context of China–Pakistan economic cooperation under the BRI.

title: Visual Information and Geographic Reliability in Residential Valuation: A Multimodal, Multi-Source Benchmark from Shanghai — analysis code and aggregate results
abstract: Companion analysis code and aggregate results for “Visual Information and Geographic Reliability in Residential Valuation: A Multimodal, Multi-Source Benchmark from Shanghai” by Cong Xu, Xinwei Gao and Jinglan Hu. Version 1.0.0. This deposit contains 22 analysis scripts, aggregate model/fold/protocol metrics, calibration and spatial residual diagnostics, measurement and external linkage summaries, extended predictor and temporal evaluation results, data dictionaries, provenance, and a Python standard-library replay script. The primary benchmark evaluates 17,716 Shanghai residential community records across 16 districts and 14,908 image footprints. The public replay checks aggregate consistency and package integrity; it does not retrain models or reconstruct individual predictions. Raw community and transaction records, exact locations, third-party RGB/GIS inputs, image patches and embeddings, row-level predictions and split assignments, and model weights are excluded because redistribution rights were not established. A distance-risk bin with n=1 is suppressed. See DATA_ACCESS.md for the source and access boundaries. This is a code and aggregate-results deposit, not a fully open raw-data replication package. Mixed-date predictors and unresolved source dates limit prospective and causal interpretations. Licensing: author-generated aggregate data and documentation are CC BY 4.0; analysis/replay code is MIT. These licences do not extend to excluded third-party inputs or dependencies. AI-assisted development with ChatGPT/Codex and Claude is documented in the package. Funding: National Social Science Fund of China, General Project, grant 24BJY144. Research contact: xuc14@qdhhc.edu.cn.

title: EVOLUTION OF THE SHANGHAI COOPERATION ORGANISATION: FROM THE "SHANGHAI FIVE" TO A MULTIFUNCTIONAL INTERNATIONAL ORGANISATION
abstract: The evolution of the SCO from a border confidence-building mechanism to a multifunctional intergovernmental organisation is examined. The stages of the “Shanghai Five”, the establishment of the SCO, institutionalisation, the expansion of functions and membership, and the strategic renewal of 2025-2026 are identified. It is shown that the organisation developed through consensus, permanent bodies and sectoral coordination without transferring sovereign powers to supranational structures.

title: Cell-level verification package for a study of public EV charging supply and taxi-derived carbon activity in central Shanghai (500 m grid, 1,494 cells)
abstract: This record holds the verification material for a manuscript under peer review at Sustainable Cities and Society (manuscript SCSI-D-26-08252). It is deposited so that the handling editor can trace every quantity printed in the submission back to the file and the code it came from. Access to the files is restricted during review. The deposit is a single archive, SCSI-D-26-08252_verification_bundle.zip (23,935,675 bytes, MD5 108ae28c0462d49f81f5b4d43d58f41a). It contains a README, a manifest listing the MD5 of every file, and the two packages submitted with the revision, stored unmodified and byte for byte: 1. Editor_package.zip (731 files, MD5 bed0f0198b1c795e00a91a9d1eb95aa2) — the reproduction package. Its anchor table registers each reported quantity together with the result file it was read from, that file's checksum, the script that produced it and the line range within that script (411 rows). Alongside it are the cell-level derived data and the result files the table names, the analysis, figure and verification code, the near-neighbour literature screening record, and the grid shapefile whose attribute table holds the 1,494 cell-level records used in the analysis. Folder names, the anchor table, the data dictionary, the screening record and all documentation an editor needs to read are in English; code comments and printed reports remain in the authors' working language, with a glossary provided. 2. Confidential_verification_package.zip (5 files, MD5 6c1d7ffcc593eb3f6c150721c4870a19) — the confidential verification files: a field dictionary of the taxi GPS data and of the derived trip table, including the observed value domain of the occupancy flag on which the carbon accounting rests; a before-and-after table of every headline quantity set against its value in the initial submission (28 rows); and the aggregate outputs of five checks of the occupancy coding. Study context. Public charging supply in the seven central districts of Shanghai is measured in two ways — installed capacity, and capacity per resident reachable within 1 km — and each is compared against a taxi-derived internal-combustion-equivalent carbon activity field built from peak-period taxi travel. The unit of analysis is a 500 m cell (1,494 cells, EPSG:32651). What is not included. The raw positional records behind the carbon accounting and the commercial point-of-interest snapshot behind the supply measure are not redistributed. The deposit holds the derived, cell-level quantities and the code that produces them, not those upstream inputs; the manuscript's data availability statement states the applicable access restrictions. Integrity. MANIFEST.tsv inside the archive lists the size and MD5 of each embedded package and of every file within them, so that the contents can be confirmed to be the files registered with the submission. Access. Files are restricted for the duration of peer review and will be opened on acceptance.
